frase_gancho.texto: A basalt portrait more than three thousand years old: the face of an Olmec king.

puente_narrativo.texto: Power could also lie in movement. Now look for a seated figure of dark stone, twisting its torso as if it had been caught in the middle of a gesture.

guion_corto.texto: In front of you is a stone head almost one meter seventy tall, carved from a single block of basalt more than three thousand years ago. It is Colossal Head number six from San Lorenzo, one of the seventeen known from the Olmec culture. It is not a god or a monster: it is thought to be the portrait of a ruler. Notice the features: full cheeks, a broad nose, thick lips, and almond-shaped eyes. He wears a close-fitting helmet, perhaps of leather, with ear protectors. Each head has its own features, so each one was, it seems, a different king. The basalt came from the Tuxtlas mountains, more than sixty kilometers from here.

guion_largo.texto:
Some works seem modern because of their power, and this is one of them. It was carved centuries before the Zapotecs founded Monte Albán, and it belongs to the Olmec, the first great culture of Mesoamerica. This head is their calling card: a human face, enormous and serene, that has gazed at us for more than three thousand years.

The name “Olmec” has a curious history. The Mexica used it for the people of the Gulf Coast of their own time: “people of the rubber country,” from olli, rubber. Centuries later, archaeologists used the same name for this much older culture, whose own name for itself we do not know. Rubber, the latex of a tropical tree, was their great source of wealth. The oldest rubber balls found in Mexico, at El Manatí, Veracruz, are about three thousand six hundred years old.

Seventeen colossal heads are known, spread among San Lorenzo, La Venta, and other sites. All of them are different: each has its own features and its own helmet, and for that reason they are thought to be portraits of rulers. There is even an idea, still debated, that some were sculpted from old stone thrones, reused when the king died.

Now think about how the material got here. Basalt is not found at San Lorenzo: it comes from the Tuxtlas mountains, more than sixty kilometers away. This stone weighs several tons, and the Olmec had no wheels or pack animals. It is thought they moved it with rafts along rivers and swamps, with rollers, and with a great many people, perhaps hundreds. Whoever gave the orders could move a mountain this way. That ability to organize people was also a form of power.

Look at the helmet. Fitted close to the head, with ear protectors and a band across the forehead, it resembles the equipment of the ball game, and some researchers think it could be that, or a war helmet. Each head wears a different one: a kind of identification. You will see the ball game again a little further on.

Was this the “mother culture”? That is what Alfonso Caso called it in 1942, the same person who discovered the tombs of Monte Albán. Today many archaeologists prefer to speak of a “sister culture”: other peoples of Oaxaca, Chiapas, and the Highlands developed at the same time and influenced one another. What is certain is that the Olmec style traveled very far. You already saw its mark at Tlapacoya and Tlatilco, in the baby face, and at San José Mogote, in Oaxaca.

One last curiosity: around the year nine hundred BC, many monuments at San Lorenzo were mutilated and buried. We do not know whether it was a revolt, a ritual to “kill” the monuments, or a change of power. This head survived.

Look at it head-on for a moment. It has no body, no throne, no inscription. And even so, after three thousand years, it still looks like a face with character.

texto.Origin: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán, municipality of Texistepec, Veracruz
texto.Dimensions: 1.67 m high x 1.41 m wide x 0.99 m thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: The colossal heads represent gods.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are thought to be portraits of rulers: each one has its own features and a different helmet, like an identification.
